02 · Desk research

Is this problem worth 16 days?

Before talking to anyone, I spent a weekend with industry reports and eye-tracking literature to check the problem was real — and to write a sharper interview guide.

~76%of purchase decisions are made in-store, at the shelfPOPAI shopper engagement studies
$25–60ktypical cost of one eye-tracking store study, 6–10 week lead timevendor quotes, desk notes
1–2 / yrbehavioral studies a mid-size retail team actually budgets forconfirmed later in interviews

RQ1 — What does one round of shopper insight actually cost, and where does the money go?

answered by desk research

RQ2 — Which deliverables change stakeholder decisions, and which get ignored?

answered in interviews

RQ3 — How does being observed change how people shop?

answered in interviews + WOz
The gap: everything with real store context costs lab money. The desk research gave me three questions to pressure-test in interviews — cost, deliverables, and participant behavior.

04 · Interviews → affinity map

Five conversations, one wall

The desk research said the problem was cost. The interviews said something better: cost was only a third of it.

“I get one in-store study a year if I'm lucky. The rest of the year I'm guessing from surveys.”

Senior UX Researcher · grocery retail

“The data is never the problem. Getting stakeholders to feel what the shopper felt — that's the problem.”

Shopper-insights lead · CPG

“They put a camera on my head and I stopped acting like myself immediately.”

Study participant · P3

“Cost kills frequency”

eye-tracking rig = $$$ + a technician
recruiting for in-store takes weeks
store won't close for a study
insight arrives after the layout ships

“Data isn't a story”

heatmap PNGs get one slide, then die
nobody reads the CSV
stakeholders trust video, not charts
“show me the moment she gave up”

“Participants perform”

headsets make people self-conscious
observers change behavior
think-aloud dies after 5 min
games make people forget the lab
48 notes from 5 interviews, clustered in FigJam over two evenings. Each cluster became an insight; each insight drove a later method.

Context is the product

Researchers don't want another survey tool — they want the store, with instruments hidden inside it. → drove the landscape map

Replay beats reports

The deliverable that moves stakeholders is re-living a session, not reading its summary. → drove the card sort & results IA

Invisible instrumentation

Every visible sensor changes behavior. The game is the disguise the sensors wear. → became the riskiest assumption to test

05 · Competitive landscape

Where nothing sits

Insight 01 said context is the product — so I mapped every existing method by how much store context it keeps versus what it costs.

Audit of 6 approaches. The empty corner was the opportunity — but claiming it rested on assumptions nobody had checked. That's the next board.
06 · Assumption mapping

What has to be true?

An empty quadrant is either an opportunity or a graveyard. Before designing anything I listed every assumption behind “3D store in a browser” and sorted them by evidence and risk.

Assumption map. Top-right is where projects die — so the two guesses up there got dedicated methods: a Wizard-of-Oz pilot (§09) and an emotion-validity check (§12).
Riskiest assumption

“Participants will behave naturally — and keep thinking aloud — inside a game-like store.” If this is false, every heatmap the tool produces is fiction. It became the thing every later test round watched for.

07 · Personas & jobs

Two people to design for

The interviews kept splitting into two voices — the person running the study and the person inside it. I made them personas, then sharpened each into a job story.

M

Maya, 34

Senior UX Researcher · runs 20+ studies/yr

“I need evidence I can walk into a Tuesday meeting with.”

Goals
  • Test layout ideas before they're built
  • Show stakeholders the shopper's experience
  • Run 10 participants in a week, not a quarter
Frictions
  • Lab studies need budget approval
  • Data exports nobody opens
  • Tools that need IT to install
D

Devon, 27

Study participant · does 2–3 panels a month

“If it feels like a test, I act like I'm being tested.”

Goals
  • Get in, do the thing, get the incentive
  • Feel normal, not observed
  • Know exactly what's being recorded
Frictions
  • Camera permission = instant suspicion
  • Long setup before anything happens
  • Talking to no one feels weird
Job story · Maya

When a layout decision is looming, I want believable behavioral evidence within a week, so I can shape the decision before it ships — not audit it afterward.

Job story · Devon

When I join a study, I want to know what's recorded and then just play, so I can act like myself and finish inside my lunch break.

Personas are fictional composites of the five interviewees — no stock faces on principle. The two job stories became the yardstick for every scope cut in §08.

Who else has a stake

Ethics review earned an early spot — the tool records faces and voices, which shaped how the onboarding asks for each permission.

The participant's ride

I walked three pilot users through a paper version of the flow and charted Devon's emotional ride. The deepest dip decided the next two months of onboarding work.

Journey map from pilot walkthroughs. The permissions dip is the emotional floor — its three opportunity notes rewrote themselves as the HMWs below.
HMW 01 ← journey dipHow might we make being studied feel like playing?
HMW 02 ← insight 02How might a researcher walk through a session that already happened?
HMW 03 ← maya's jobHow might a store layout become as editable as a text file?
08 · Design principles

Three rules I didn't break

Each HMW collapsed into a principle — the tie-breakers for every argument I had with myself for the rest of the build.

The game is the disguise.

Every sensor hides inside play. If a participant can feel the instrument, the instrument is wrong.

The store is a text file.

Iteration speed beats visual fidelity. A layout change must never require a 3D tool.

Data must replay as a story.

The output is not a chart. It's the researcher stepping back into the session.

✦
North-star metric: time-to-insight

Minutes from “participant clicks the link” to “researcher watches the moment that matters.” Every scope decision below was scored against this number — guardrails: session completion rate and participant comfort.

09 · Crazy 8s → prioritization

Eight bets, one budget

With principles as judges, I sketched eight ways to capture shopper behavior in eight minutes — then scored every sketch against a 16-day solo budget.

Crazy 8s, redrawn from my notebook. Then every sketch got a dot on the impact/effort board:
Everything left of the dashed line shipped: the store, the replay, voice nudges — and the 2D heat view survived as the bird's-eye camera toggle. AR and VR went to the parking lot, not the trash.
10 · Wizard of Oz

I was the voice agent

The riskiest assumption (§05) and the “think-aloud dies” sticky both pointed at the same cheap experiment: before writing any voice code, I played the agent.

Three participants shopped a clickable mock store on a screen share. Behind the curtain, I read nudges from a six-line script whenever they went quiet for ~10 seconds. They believed it was software.

The wizard's script (excerpt)

“What are you looking for right now?” · silence > 10s

“Say whatever's in your head — there's no wrong answer.” · first silence only

“What did you expect to find there?” · after a backtrack

✗ “The beans are in aisle 3.” · never help — it ends the data

n=3, scrappy on purpose. The result justified building the real agent — and set its rules: voice-activity detection, nudges not answers, max 4 interventions per session.
11 · Card sorting → results IA

How researchers think about a session

Insight 02 said replay beats reports — but the results page still needed a structure. I gave 5 researchers 28 cards of “everything a session produces” and asked them to sort.

“Moments” 5/5 AGREED
timeline of snapshots
what they said (transcript)
emotion at each moment
task started / completed
“Space” 5/5 AGREED
gaze heatmap
walked path
3D replay of the store
items collected
“Evidence” 4/5 AGREED
audio recording
session metadata
AI summary — 3/5 put it here, 2/5 threw it out
Open card sort, n=5, remote. Two findings restructured the page: moments and space are different mental models (→ timeline and 3D replay became separate views, cross-linked), and nobody trusted the AI summary as a headline (→ demoted below the timeline, framed as “draft notes”).
Lo-fi wireframe straight from the sort: Moments rail on top, Space as a portal into the 3D replay, audio as the sync spine, AI summary demoted. This shipped nearly unchanged.

The whole service on one page

With both sides defined — Devon's session and Maya's results — a service blueprint checked that every frontstage moment had its backstage machinery, before any of it got built.

Service blueprint, drawn before the build sprint. The two red-flag columns — permissions and results — are exactly where the journey map predicted the emotional dips.
12 · Build

The store is typed, not modeled

HMW 03 demanded a store as editable as text — so that's literally what I built. This is the shipped store's actual source file, and the paint is the real gaze-heat scale. Try it.

layout.txt — production sourcemove your cursor = gaze
Editing an aisle is a text edit. Testing a second layout is a git diff — which is what makes §13 possible at all.
The system in one picture. Because the world is deterministic from text, a full session replay weighs kilobytes.
Round 2 · the plot twist
“By minute three, they weren't shopping anymore — they were painting.”

Participants discovered their own gaze turned blocks red — and turned the instrument into a toy. The fix wasn't a better heatmap. It was admitting that researcher and participant need different products sharing one screen.

13 · Usability testing × 3

Three rounds, three humbling lessons

Every round went hunting for the riskiest assumption from §05 — “people behave naturally.” Round 2 found exactly how it breaks.

Round 1 — moderated

n=4 · in person · think-aloud
  • The tutorial exhausted everyone. 11 gated micro-steps before the store; 2 of 4 asked “how much longer?”
  • Opposing keys sped players up — a movement math bug surfaced by a participant mashing W+S.
  • Mic permission was a wall. One flat refusal = whole session dead at the time.

Round 2 — remote

n=6 · unmoderated · recorded
  • Participants gamed the heatmap. They saw blocks redden under their gaze — and started painting. The data was contaminating itself, live.
  • Heat saturated in 83ms in first person — every glance read as a stare. The map was binary.
  • Think-aloud died by minute 6 unless the voice agent nudged — the Wizard-of-Oz finding, confirmed in production.

Round 3 — peer critique

design review · 485-line revision
  • Onboarding restructured after an outside designer walked the funnel cold.
  • Results page reorganized around the timeline, matching the card-sort model.
  • The block grammar got documented — if a system needs me in the room, it isn't a system yet.
Small-n honesty: 4 and 6 participants. But the direction was unambiguous, and SUS crossing the 68 line between rounds was the go-signal for the pilot study in §13.
11-step gated tutorial3 checklist panels, any orderpermissions · movement · emotion check — verified by doing, not reading
Heatmap visible to participantsParticipant mode: paint silentlythe same data records; the feedback loop that invited gaming is gone
Mic refusal ends the sessionGraceful downgrade, data flaggedgaze + path + emotion still record; the session survives
Glance = stare (83ms saturation)Dwell-calibrated heat, both camerasrates normalized per second so first- and third-person data compare

Checking the second risky assumption: is webcam emotion real?

The assumption map (§05) also flagged emotion data. So during Round 2 I collected both streams — self-reported emotion buttons and webcam inference — and compared them moment by moment.

Validity check, Round 2 data. The tool now treats AI emotion as a second witness, not a verdict.
14 · The payoff — A/B layout pilot

The instrument, doing its job

Sixteen days earlier this was a HMW sticky: “a store as editable as a text file.” The final study is the receipt — two layouts, one git diff apart.

Layout A — control
xxssssssssssxx x x x x xxffffffffffxx endcap: sauce
Layout B — endcap swap (one line changed)
xxssssssssssxx x x x x xxffffffffffxx endcap: snacks ★
+38%dwell on the swapped endcap (B vs A)
−12%traffic past aisle 2
≈ sametime-to-find target items
12sessions · 6 per layout
Pilot-scale (n=6+6) — not publishable, but that was never the point. The point: a layout experiment that costs a retail team $50k took me one edited line and an afternoon of sessions.
15 · Outcome

Shipped, live, replayable

Endermax runs at endermax.com — a participant clicks a link, shops for two items, and the researcher walks back through everything the session recorded.

12pilot sessions recorded
~25 mininvite → finished session
< 60 ssession end → 3D replay
$0hardware per participant

What I'd tell past me

Your visualization can poison your data. The heatmap was the demo's best feature and the study's worst bug. Researcher-facing and participant-facing are different products sharing one screen — split them early.

The cheapest method answered the scariest question. A three-person Wizard-of-Oz test with a six-line script de-risked the entire voice agent before a line of code existed. Rank methods by risk killed per hour.

The boring file format was the best design decision. A store you can type is a store you can diff — and a store you can diff is a store you can A/B. Fidelity impresses; iteration speed wins.

16 · Where it goes next

The roadmap the testing wrote

Participant mode

Ship the heatmap-gaming fix properly: heat records silently for participants, renders only for researchers.

Session library & study links

Keep every session, name participants, and mint shareable study URLs with configurable tasks — beans and chicken were always placeholders.

Remote data collection

Sessions currently live in the participant's browser. Uploading them turns a demo into a research platform — consent flow first.

Ted Dessert — research, design, and build. Live at endermax.com.
